endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Consider the following factors when decommissioning GAI systems: Data retention requirements;

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether adding generative AI systems to an inventory with GAI-specific fields reduces untracked use or its downstream risks, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on one voluntary federal framework, NIST AI 600-1, whose quoted text addresses decommissioning and data retention rather than inventory entry fields.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single endorsement comes from a framework document and reflects expert judgment. The quoted passage concerns decommissioning factors, which makes it indirect support for the specific inventory fields named in the recommendation.

NIST AI 600-1 uses "should" language and carries no binding force, so adopting this practice is voluntary under the supplied sources. The quoted text asks organizations to consider data retention requirements at decommissioning. This suggests the framework treats lifecycle records as expected, though the excerpt does not itself specify known issues, oversight roles, versioning, or provenance fields.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems with and without GAI-specific inventory fields and measure the share of generative AI tools that go undiscovered, the time to detect and act on known issues or version changes, and incidents traced to untracked tools. Even a descriptive study of how often generative AI use goes unrecorded in current inventories would establish the size of the hazard.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot tell from the supplied sources whether inventory gaps fall more heavily on tools used with these patients, such as translation or patient-messaging tools.
